body_excerpt: These last days I tried to implement the paper [Stream-K: Work-centric Parallel Decomposition for Dense Matrix-Matrix Multiplication on the GPU](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.03598.pdf) in Triton. The main idea is to avoid wave quantization by evenly distributing work across SM using a lower granularity than a full tile. I suppose you have seen/read it, if not I can share my notes about it to help understand what I hope to achieve. It has been implemented in cutlass where it shows strong performances. The implementation below in Triton works, aka it generates the right output (minus rounding issues when K is big because of half precision, nothing unexpected). repository: rapidsai/cudf
title: [BUG] Consider disabling managed memory in cudf.pandas on WSL2
github_labels: bug
body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** cudf.pandas turns on a managed pool allocator by default to support larger-than-memory workloads. However, this does not work on WSL2 because UVM on Windows does not actually allow oversubscription. Moreover, using UVM could result in far worse slowdowns on WSL2 than observed on Windows due to how it is implemented on that platform. **Expected behavior** We should consider changing cudf.pandas to only enable managed memory by default when oversubscription is properly supported. This can be done by querying the CUDA driver for the appropriate attribute. In addition, we should run some benchmarks to evaluate the relative performance impact of using managed memory on WSL2 in undersubscribed situations

repository: rapidsai/cudf
title: CUDA reductions should have independent input and output types
github_labels: feature request|libcudf
body_excerpt: To enable higher-accuracy reductions, we should consider rewriting the internal reductions code to have independent input and accumulation/output datatypes. When summing integer types (e.g. Int8), the sum can be much larger than the input datatype can represent. So for higher accuracy one might want to use a 32-bit or 64-bit type for the accumulation and result. This is what Numpy does for `sum()` with integer types. In fact, it automatically uses the machine default integer size unless the user specifies the datatype. https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.sum.html "dtype : dtype, optional The type of the returned array and of the accumulator in which the elements are summed. title: Improved docs for (default) matmul precision
github_labels: enhancement|documentation
body_excerpt: 1. It is somewhat unintuitive that the default matmul precision is bfloat16 on TPU, especially for users coming from PyTorch/GPU where the default precision is float32. body_excerpt: `jax.random.truncated_normal` produces deeply wrong results when you set the lower bound too high or the upper bound too low. For example, ```python jax.random.truncated_normal( jax.random.PRNGKey(1), jnp.array([5., 5.25, 5.5]), 1e6, (3,)) ``` results in ``` DeviceArray([5.1665773e+00, 9.9999994e+05, 9.9999994e+05], dtype=float32) ``` The transition is suspiciously close to the point at which `erf` runs out of precision: ```python lax.erf(jnp.array([5., 5.25, 5.5]) / np.sqrt(2)) ``` gives ``` DeviceArray([0.9999994, 1. , 1. ], dtype=float32) ``` So this may be a fundamental limitation of the sampling-by-inversion scheme used in `truncated_normal`.

repository: pytorch/pytorch
title: Ctx or at least Thread level switch for fp32 IEEE precision tolerance
github_labels: module: docs|module: cuda|triaged|enhancement|module: multithreading
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Right now fp precision switching is only possible at the `process` level via the following api: ```python torch.backends.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.rnn.fp32_precision = mode ``` With Python 3.13/3.14 and `GIL=0` threads, it is now possile to do everything `torch.distributed` can do but using threads instead of processes. Without a `ctx` or `thread` level toggle for `fp` precision, it not possible to have different threads doing different tasks. For example, an `inference` thread does not need high precision whereas a `quantization` thread which often need fp32 or higher accumulation will need full `ieee` precision. They cannot co-exist currently in torch due to this limitation. ### Alternatives Use `processes`. However, this is not a true alternative since with Python 3.14, we have stable `nogil` threads that can do concurrent work as efficiently if not more so than `processes`. cc @svekars @sekyondaMeta @AlannaBurke @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @jerryzh168 @albanD @pragupta

For example, ``` import os os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = "" import jax.numpy as jnp arr = jnp.array([1, 2, 0, 0]) positions = jnp.arange(arr.shape[0]) new_arr = jnp.zeros_like(arr) new_arr = new_arr.at[positions].set(arr) print(new_arr) ``` prints the expected `[1 2 0 0]`, while setting the xla_gpu_deterministic_ops flag to true as ``` import os os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = "--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true" import jax.numpy as jnp arr = jnp.array([1, 2, 0, 0]) positions = jnp.arange(arr.shape[0]) new_arr = jnp.zeros_like(arr) new_arr = new_arr.at[positions].set(arr) print(new_arr) ``` returns `[0, 2, 0, 0]`. repository: pytorch/pytorch
title: Enabling GPU mixed precision algorithms
github_labels: triaged|module: linear algebra
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch PyTorch does not seem to provide wrappers to mixed precision algorithms in e.g MAGMA (dshpov, shportf) and cuSolver (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cusolver/index.html#cusolverirsrefinement-t). Does anyone know if that is really the case? It would be interesting to have access to these routines since these may potentially improve performance of linear system solving by a factor 4.7 using GPUs with negligible changes in the accuracy (https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/19M1298263). I created two rough prototypes for the changes that would be needed to make those mixed precision algorithms available. It seems to be a simple modification. My prototype works by changing the behavior of functions cholesky_solve (for using the dshpov MAGMA routine) and linalg.cholesky (for using the shportf MAGMA routine). Due to my lack of deep knowledge of PyTorch, I was unable to go further. It would be really awesome if someone could work on top of these prototypes to make a proper pull request. One package that could benefit from these additions would be GPyTorch, since it executes Cholesky factorizations repeatedly during its training and prediction procedure...

body_excerpt: I'd like to be able to use cuML to calculate the precision score of an estimator in Python. I didn't see a C++/CUDA implementation in the `metrics/` header files, so this may require both C++/CUDA and Python/Cython bindings eventually. Didn't see an existing issue but will close if I find one. Currently, this requires going to the CPU if we want to use an existing API (relying on NEP-18 for dispatch doesn't work here). With about three million rows, sklearn's `precision_score` can take about 1.5 seconds. A stopgap GPU implementation for binary precision using CuPy can be 500x+ faster. ```python def cupy_precision_score(y, y_pred): pos_pred_ix = cupy.where(y_pred == 1) tp_sum = (y_pred[pos_pred_ix] == y[pos_pred_ix]).sum() fp_sum = (y_pred[pos_pred_ix] != y[pos_pred_ix]).sum() ​ return (tp_sum / (tp_sum + fp_sum)).item() ​ %time print(cupy_precision_score(y, yp.values)) %time print(precision_score(y_host, y_pred)) 0.9998934583422118 CPU times: user 2.59 ms, sys: 0 ns, total: 2.59 ms Wall time: 2.05 ms 0.9998934583422118 CPU times: user 1.47 s, sys: 59.5 ms, total: 1.53 s Wall time: 1.5 s ``` Cross-listing to the tracking issue #608

repository: rapidsai/cuml
title: Avoid Hard-Coded Values in SHAP Tests

title: Refactor precision handling in test/test_optim.py
github_labels: module: optimizer|triaged|better-engineering|actionable
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently, there are scattered places in the optimizer tests that reduce precision (grepping for `atol` or `rtol` in the file will take you to those places). Since optimizers are a composition of ATen ops, they reasonably require higher tolerances. Thus, we should establish a per optimizer (and perhaps per dtype) tolerance at the top level of the test file and use that everywhere. This consolidation has (at least) two functions: - Define an agreed upon set of expected tolerances for optimizers - Enable ease when writing new optimizer tests that will inevitably run into the same tolerance issues. One way to do this is to override assertEqual in the Optimizer TestCase class. ### Alternatives Another way is to globally define them and then pass them whenever needed. This seems a more manual way to get the same results as overriding though. ### Additional context I'm in the middle of migrating tests from test/optim/test_optim.py to test/test_optim.py. title: DeepSeek: mixed precision optimizers (BF16AdamW)
github_labels: module: optimizer|triaged
body_excerpt: DeepSeek mentions that they keep optimizer states in bf16, this is something that afaik our optimizers don't support. Similarly, one could imagine computing/accumulating gradients in less than fp32 accuracy and adding them to fp32 params, something that's also not supported today, when `param` and `param.grad` are mandated to have the same dtype, and by default optimizers operate on `param` and `param.grad`. That can be worked around with functional invocation, but we don't have convenient constructs to do that. Insufficient optimizer flexibility might be one of the reasons a lot of projects start by copying optimizer wholesale and modifying it for their needs. cc @vincentqb @jbschlosser @albanD @janeyx99 @crcrpar

title: [MPS] For accumulating ops allow the correctness tolerance to scale within the envelope of the reference implementations drift
github_labels: module: tests|triaged|enhancement|module: half|module: mps|bot-triaged
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Context Related to the discussion at issue #182817 this is an orthogonal issue with the current testing approach and a suggestion on how we could address it: When testing op correctness for fp16/bf16 implementations in MPS backend we compare against the CPU computations done with the same precision. For ops that aggregate multiple computations to produce the elements of the final result like convolutions or reduction ops the ordering how the computation happens will cause a drift in the final product. One can estimate the worst case per-element error with `err = sqrt(K) * eps * |x|` where `K` is the reduction depth, `eps` the machine epsilon for the dtype and `|x|` the partial product magnitude. So this tells us that the expected uncertainty grows with the number of partial results aggregated as well as machine epsilon that is orders of magnitude larger for fp16 and bf16 compared to fp32. repository: pytorch/pytorch
title: Raise exception when torch.clamp min value underflows the input tensor's dtype
github_labels: module: error checking|triaged
body_excerpt: Consider the following code: ```python x = torch.relu(torch.randn(10)) x = torch.clamp(x, min=1e-8) y = 100 / x ``` The code above runs just fine when `x.dtype == torch.float` but fails when `x.dtype == torch.half`. The error is that 1e-8 can't be represented in fp16 and silently underflows to 0. Depending on the network it can be difficult to track down the source of this class of error (especially if a network was originally written assuming fp32 and is then trained with mixed precision). Could we validate inputs for potential underflows and raise an exception if one is detected?

title: Allow explicit matmul precision
github_labels: enhancement
body_excerpt: This is a proposal to improve and generalize [jax.lax.Precision](https://jax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/jax.lax.html#jax.lax.Precision). The current design has a number of limitations: 1. Its difficult to write device-independent code, as `jax.lax.Precision` means different numerics on different hardware (eg. `jax.lax.Precision.DEFAULT` with FP32 inputs does matmul in FP32 on V100, TF32 on A100/H100, BF16 on TPUs), which is a major user footgun for porting JAX functions between TPU/GPU. 2. Its not general enough to support alternative matmul precision modes. For example, [CUTLASS supports faster FP32 matmul via 3-pass TF32](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/examples/27_ampere_3xtf32_fast_accurate_tensorop_gemm/27_ampere_3xtf32_fast_accurate_tensorop_gemm.cu). github_labels: bug
body_excerpt: ### Description Since `jaxlib` 0.5.3, I get a different behavior of the autodiff result for equivalent functions. One function does broadcasting while the other explicitly repeats indices for indexing. body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** The [`THROW`](https://github.com/rapidsai/cuml/blob/branch-0.10/cpp/src_prims/utils.h#L84) macro is using a fixed size buffer to form the message for an exception. This is unsafe because the buffer could easily be overflowed by a particularly long error message. **Expected behavior** `THROW` should not use a fixed size buffer, nor should it use `printf`s. See [`CUDF_EXPECTS`](https://github.com/rapidsai/cudf/blob/branch-0.10/cpp/src/utilities/error_utils.hpp#L90) for how we do the same thing in a safe way. **Additional context** A common set of error catching macros like this is probably something that should eventually live in RAPIDS core to avoid issues like this in the future.

title: jaxlib: malformed pickled PyTreeDef can crash flatten_up_to
github_labels: bug
body_excerpt: `PyTreeDef` pickle state includes cached per-node bookkeeping fields: ```text (kind, arity, node_data, custom_type, num_leaves, num_nodes) ``` `PyTreeDef.__setstate__` / `FromPickle` currently restores those cached `num_leaves` and `num_nodes` values directly. If a malformed pickle sets the final node's `num_leaves` to `-2147483648`, a later call to `flatten_up_to()` can crash the process instead of raising a Python exception. The crash happens because `FlattenUpTo` uses `num_leaves()` both to allocate the output list and to initialize the leaf write index: ```cpp nb::list leaves = nb::steal<nb::list>(PyList_New(num_leaves())); ... int leaf = num_leaves() - 1; ``` For `INT_MIN`, `PyList_New()` returns null, while `num_leaves() - 1` overflows to a large positive value on typical release builds. body_excerpt: One of the challenges with providing optimized primitives for sparse datasets is the large number of different degree distributions that can be encountered in practice. In some recent discussions with @teju85 @beckernick @VibhuJawa @aerdem4 and @randerzander, we have isolated some potential upper bounds specific to the string matching use-case which can offer some additional memory savings (and potential performance boost) by performing the k-select in the same kernel that's computing distances. What has been discussed so far is that the number of tokens per row for string matching could very well be bounded from above by a few hundred to a few thousand. For metrics which can be 1. implemented in expanded form (such as cosine), and 2. where the max degree of any row can fit into shared memory in sparse form, we only require a single pass through the distance kernel. repository: triton-lang/triton
title: feat(examples): implement vllm in triton
github_labels: 
body_excerpt: Vllm uses paged memory and has kernels that perform the generation part of the causal inference. The computation pattern of generation part - single Q for entire seq len of KV - is very different from computing the context part (which benefits from seq length parallelism over Q and hence flash attention). In this case, the bottleneck should be memory, as the KV values cannot be reused over the Q seq len, so it is an interesting question to ask how to tradeoff latency and parallelism with compute efficiency. In this case, batching similar seq length inference is very important. I also wonder if distributed shared memory and TMA optimizations would be beneficial here since it is so memory-bottlenecked. It would be interesting to implement this in triton and see whether triton can match or exceed the performance. Reference VLLM implementation here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d2b2eed67c49cdda3c1d6fa09ee2ec128b318138/csrc/attention/attention_kernels.cu#L32

title: [CodeGen] LLVM codegen doesn't respect mfloat-abi=hard
github_labels: 
body_excerpt: For versions of LLVM < 6.0, the mfloat-abi=hard flag does not appear to be respected resulting in operators such as exp and softmax giving incorrect results on Raspberry Pi 3. repository: apache/tvm
title: [Bug] Padded, quantized convolution operators give incorrect results on edges
github_labels: type: bug|needs-triage
body_excerpt: When the microTVM team was working on our submission for MLPerf Tiny, we noticed the `kws` model had slightly worse accuracy than expected (we classified `897/1000` samples correctly, while folks are expected to classify [at least `900/1000` correctly](https://github.com/mlcommons/tiny/tree/master/benchmark)). The bug has been remarkably hard to track down. We have a bunch of [end-to-end operator](https://github.com/apache/tvm/tree/main/tests/python/relay/strategy/arm_cpu/) tests, and our results match exactly with those in other parts of TVM. I originally thought this was a padding issue, but that didn't pan out. It turns out the issue is caused by a bugged optimization for re-quantization. This issue only occurs in quantization (which is why our tests didn't catch it - those don't include quantization steps), and only on the edges of padded tensors (which explains why it hurt accuracy slightly, but not a ton). I've written up an explanation of the issue below. cc @alanmacd @areusch @gromero @mehrdadh @mkatanbaf

body_excerpt: ## Motivation The following work is done jointly by me and my team @kaitingwang at Huawei Canada. The TritonGPUCoalesce pass generates blocked layouts for load/stores that favour memory coalescing and vectorization. However, we have observed in certain cases the blocked layout generate by TritonGPUCoalesce pass is suboptimal and results in generation of `convert_layout` instructions. When these `convert_layout` are generated inside a loop, it could negatively impact performance. body_excerpt: This issue serves as a backup of some ideas discussed in the Gitter room. # Result caching in combination with Numba ## Premise One clear application of numba is the speedup of costly computations. Besides acceleration of such computations, it could be useful to cache results of such functions, if they are pure functions and expected to be called with the same parameters frequently. The Python standard library offers e.g. the [lru_cache in the functools module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.lru_cache), which memoises the most recent calls of the functions it is wrapping. ## Challenge At the current time, no best practice or recipe exists for how to efficiently combine numba's jit capabilities and a caching approach. If only a single function is to be compiled by numba and have its results cached, this can be achieved efficiently by wrapping the jit or njit compiled function with the lru_cache like ```python @lru_cache() @njit def add_one(x): return x+1 ``` The problem arises when we want to call a (jitted and) cached, function from a another jitted function as in ```python @jit def foo(x) return bar(x) @lru_cache() @jit def bar(x) return x + 1 ``` Th...

repository: cupy/cupy
title: Implement cupy.ndarray == None and cupy.ndarray != None
github_labels: issue-checked

The pre-softmax scores can reach ~2.5 × 10²¹ — still within float32 range. Numerically stable softmax (`exp(x − max(x)) / Σ exp(x − max(x))`) should handle this correctly. title: Inductor generates redundant upcast_to_fp32

body_excerpt: ## 🐛 Describe the bug `TritonOverrides.to_dtype()` unconditionally emits `.to(out_dtype)` without checking whether the input CSE variable already has the target dtype. When `config.triton.codegen_upcast_to_fp32=True`, loads are upcast to float32 at codegen time, but the IR still emits explicit `to_dtype` nodes (since IR tracks the logical dtype bf16/fp16, not the codegen dtype). This produces redundant no-op instructions in the generated Triton kernel. ## Repro ```python import torch from torch._inductor import config from torch._inductor.utils import run_and_get_triton_code config.triton.codegen_upcast_to_fp32 = True def fn(x, y): a = x * y # bf16 * bf16 b = a.float() # explicit cast that survives to codegen return b + 1.0 x = torch.randn(4, 1024, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device='cuda') y = torch.randn(4, 1024, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device='cuda') code = run_and_get_triton_code(torch.compile(fn), x, y) print(code) ``` **Generated code (before fix):** ```python tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x0), xmask).to(tl.float32) tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (x0), xmask).to(tl.float32) tmp2 = tmp0 * tmp1 tmp3 = tmp2.to(tl.float32) # <-- REDUNDANT: tmp2 is already float32 tmp4 = tl.full([1, 1], 1.0, tl....

repository: pytorch/pytorch
title: [Inductor] F.lp_pool{1,2,3}d fail with OverflowError when norm_type=float('inf')
github_labels: triaged|oncall: pt2|module: inductor|pt2: numerics-discrepancy
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug When using `torch.compile` (Inductor backend) with `F.lp_pool1d`, `F.lp_pool2d`, or `F.lp_pool3d` setting `norm_type=float('inf')`, the code crashes with an `OverflowError` during the lowering phase. title: Support alpha=inf consistently for torch.celu
github_labels: module: nn|triaged|module: python frontend
body_excerpt: The celu activation function introduced in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.07483 is described as being C1 differentiable across values of alpha. - for alpha -> inf it converges to the identity op (f(x) = x) - for alpha -> 0+ it converges to relu(x) = max(0, x) The Pytorch [celu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/native/Activation.cpp#L538-L549) (and related [quantized_celu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qelu.cpp#L24)) ) implementation(s) appears to call a parameterized elu, following the celu definition, so it looks like it will have these properties within bounds of overflow. On the other hand I am not sure what the Pytorch behavior is intended to be in the implementation for alpha=0 and alpha=inf, but I think it would be nice to have it consistent. At alpha=0 it raises RuntimeError ZeroDivisionError, which is fine, though it seems could instead for alpha=0 just short-circuit to return relu(x). On the other hand, at alpha=torch.inf, positive values of x appear to return x, while non-positive values of x return `torch.nan`: ``` x = torch.tensor(2.) torch.celu(x, torch.inf) # tensor(2.) torch.celu(-x, torch.inf...

repository: pytorch/pytorch
title: [MPS] Complex `abs` overflows/underflows with large/small inputs
github_labels: module: numerical-stability|triaged|module: complex|module: edge cases|module: mps|bot-triaged
body_excerpt: For sufficiently large or small complex inputs, the output of `torch.abs` for MPS overflows to inf or underflows to 0, whereas the CPU op does not. This is due to the fact that the formula that the MPS op uses is $\sqrt{\text{real}^2 + \text{imag}^2}$, so the square can overflow. title: Ban GradScaler scale from being less than 1
github_labels: triaged|module: amp (automated mixed precision)
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch We should standardize on a way to tell users when a reasonable/good scale for the AMP GradScaler cannot be found. Context: The grad scaler is awesome in that it "automatically" finetunes itself to settle on an ideal scale. However! There are instances where there is just no ideal scale for certain parameters, for example the one mentioned in issue #96755, where the scale becomes so so tiny that it causes infs and, consequently, nans. In this issue, we were nestled in the unlikely (but clearly not impossible) world where for a certain scale S, the scaled gradients were valid, but the unscaled (g/S) were invalid, leading to weird inconsistent behavior. Generally, we want to be add invariants/guarantees to prevent weird inconsistent behavior and give users faster and clearer signal. Since the purpose of the scale is to scale UP the loss so that the grads do not underflow in fp16, we should set a hard boundary of scale must be greater than or equal to 1. Note that adding a check may induce a slight perf hit. cc @mcarilli @ptrblck @leslie-fang-intel @jgong5 @ngimel @crcrpar @stas00 @albanD ### Alternatives Do nothing, let users deal with nans f...

repository: pytorch/pytorch
title: `softmax` to handle dimensions comprised of `-inf`
github_labels: module: nn|triaged
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently `softmax` handles `-inf` in most of the cases, for example: ```python >>> x = torch.tensor([-float('inf'), 1]) >>> x.softmax(-1) tensor([0., 1.]) >>> x.cuda().softmax(-1) tensor([0., 1.], device='cuda:0') ``` However, once the normalized dimension is comprised of solely `-inf`, there is an issue: ```python >>> x = torch.tensor([-float('inf')] * 2) >>> x.softmax(-1) tensor([nan, nan]) >>> x.cuda().softmax(-1) tensor([nan, nan], device='cuda:0') ``` I understand we get it because `inf - inf = nan`, but why not assume that `softmax` is computed in the limit? In such a case `softmax` should return a uniform distribution. This case is quite easy to detect since `max == -inf` will imply a uniform distribution. Issues for more context: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/25110 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/103749 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/103963 cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki

body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ``` import torch import torch.nn as nn torch.manual_seed(0) fc1 = nn.Linear(8, 8) fc2 = nn.Linear(8, 8) bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(8) x = torch.randn(4, 8) with torch.enable_grad(): x = x.requires_grad_(True) x_ = fc1(x) x_ = torch.nn.functional.hardswish(x_) # can output exactly 0 x_ = bn(x_) x_ = fc2(x_) x_ = torch.log1p(x_) out = torch.xlogy(x_, x_) # xlogy(0, 0) = NaN if any element = 0 print(f"hardswish zeros: {(torch.nn.functional.hardswish(fc1(x).detach()) == 0).sum().item()}") print(f"xlogy output: nan={torch.isnan(out).any().item()}") # Minimal 3-line version: print("\nMinimal: xlogy at x=0") v = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]) print(f"xlogy(v, v) = {torch.xlogy(v, v)}") # Expected: [nan, -0.3466, 0.0, 1.3863] # NaN because xlogy(0, 0) = 0 * log(0) = 0 * -inf = NaN # The mathematically correct value: print(f"lim_{{x→0}} x*log(x) = 0, but torch gives: {torch.xlogy(torch.tensor(0.0), torch.tensor(0.0))}") ``` ### Versions 2.9.1+cu128 (PyTorch 2.9.1, CUDA 12.8) torch.xlogy(0, 0) returns NaN, while in many numerical computing libraries (e.g., SciPy) and common machine learning practice, it is defined as 0. cc @mruberry @kshitij12345

title: [jet] use proper Taylor coefficients during calculation
github_labels: enhancement
body_excerpt: In *Evaluating Derivatives* (Griewank & Walther, §13) the Taylor series in the Taylor propagation approach (i.e., `jet`) is $f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n,$ where $a_n$ is called the *n*-th Taylor coefficient. `jax.experimental.jet` instead propagates the factorial-scaled value $c_n=n! \cdot a_n$ and calls $c_n$ as the Taylor coefficient in the docs. While this makes the output of `jet` interpretable as an ordinary n-th order derivative of $f$, it forces extra scaling/un-scaling by \$n!\$, which can overflow or amplify rounding error due to the use of factorial (see #9712); **Proposal:** propagate the unscaled coefficients \$a\_n\$ internally and (optionally) offer a compatibility flag/wrapper current for the `n!` convention. Below is a comparison of the exponential rule before and after this change: ```python # Current jet implementation def _exp_taylor(primals_in, series_in, **_): x, = primals_in series, = series_in u = [x] + series v = [lax.exp(x)] + [None] * len(series) for k in range(1,len(v)): v[k] = fact(k-1) * sum(_scale(k, j) * v[k-j] * u[j] for j in range(1, k+1)) primal_out, *series_out = v return primal_out, series_out jet_rules[lax.exp_p] = _exp_taylor ``` ```pyt...

body_excerpt: @jakevdp I am trying to use float8 datatypes as part of training quantized spiking neural networks but cannot initialise weights for a network because jax.random.\_uniform does not support jnp.float8_* dtypes. My intent is to train on an H100 GPU which supports fp8 with double the throughput of fp16. The error message for jax.random.\_uniform seems to be a little out of date as well as it only discusses fp32/64 while also accepting fp16. I'm not sure how much work it would take to permit fp8 types but would greatly appreciate it! It seems that the uniform sampling method would need updated but I'm not sure how many other changes would be required to support fp8. Beyond language model applications, neuroevolution would largely benefit from fp8 because of the fact that you could double the population size for the same compute/memory capacity and SNN research would also benefit as one could represent both the input spikes and model weights in fp8 and eliminate having to recast int8 inputs to fp16 values for use. _Originally posted by @kmheckel in https://github.com/google/jax/discussions/16342#discussioncomment-6396762_

repository: jax-ml/jax
title: Implicit dtype promotion for float8 and int4
github_labels: enhancement
body_excerpt: We've had several requests to add implicit promotion semantics for float8, int4, and friends. What do i mean by this? Currently, if you try to combine `float8` with other float dtypes in binary operations, you get an error: ```python >>> jnp.float8_e3m4(1) + jnp.bfloat16(1) TypePromotionError: Input dtypes ('bfloat16', 'float8_e3m4') have no available implicit dtype promotion path. To avoid unintended promotion, 8-bit floats do not support implicit promotion. If you'd like your inputs to be promoted to another type, you can do so explicitly using e.g. x.astype('float32') ``` This was a deliberate design choice: when we first added narrow-width floats and ints, our assumption was that they would mostly be used in very particular settings, e.g. as inputs to device-specific matmul kernels, and users would benefit from having guard-rails against inadvertent type promotion. But increasingly this hard line is causing issues for users: for example, pallas has had to implement this helper to work around the lack of implicit promotion for int4 and float8: https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/3ebff21919983f87ce5dcab4cc0b27eb89b28368/jax/_src/pallas/primitives.py#L705-L711 This issue tracks ...

In order to clearly signal the semantic meaning of these variables, avoid signed/unsigned casting and comparisons, and to reduce the likelihood of overflow/underflow bugs, I propose the following rules: 1. Liberal use of `auto` should make this less onerous, and rule 1 should make it rare. 3. When representing the size of a quantity *other* than the size of a container or doing any other kind of raw positive indexing, use `std::size_t` *unless* there is a clear performance/resource reason to use a smaller type. body_excerpt: ## 🐛 Bug torch.dtype is int in JIT instead of torch.dtype. title: [FEA] Improve dtype dispatch patterns in Python
github_labels: feature request|Python|Performance|improvement
body_excerpt: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.** There are numerous places in cudf that require polymorphic behavior depending on the dtype of a parameter. Two of the most prominent are `ColumnBase.astype` and `build_column`, both of which essentially boil down to a switch statement based on the dtype. There are numerous issues with this implementation. Two of the most obvious ones are: - Performance: See #12494 - It violates the open-closed principle. There is no way to register new types. For `ColumnBase.astype`, this is managed by having the various `as_*_dtype` methods defined in `ColumnBase`, but there is no way to add a new one in general. The only real option would be to monkey-patch the method (same for `build_column`). - It violates the single responsibility principle. body_excerpt: ### Description UMAP cannot run large datasets right now because of an overflow issue. `raft::sparse::COO` defaults to using `int` for its `Index_Type` and this becomes a problem. When [this issue](https://github.com/rapidsai/raft/issues/2405) is solved, we need to update `UMAPAlgo::FuzzySimplSet::ML::run()` to take `COO` with an `Index_Type` other than `int`. ### Details Specifically, `coo_symmetrize` (raft function called from `UMAPAlgo::FuzzySimplSet::ML::run()`) allocates `nnz * 2` space on device. For a large dataset (e.g. 88M samples with knn graph degree 16) this value is larger than max int (88M * 16 * 2 > INT_MAX).

repository: pytorch/pytorch
title: dict_tag optimization leads to wrong results with relational guards
github_labels: triaged|oncall: pt2|module: dynamo
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug `dict_tag` optimization checks if a dictionary that we guard on has changed or not and if all the values in it are immutable, no further processing is done on the dictionary if the tag is the same. This avoids running a lot of guards on the dictionary and its values and makes the C++ guards faster. However this assumes that running a guard has no side-effects. This is true for almost all cases except for RelationalGuards which do keep a state. In RelationalGuards, we need 2 values for the guards and the way it works is that the guard returns True for the first run, stores the first value in the guard and only returns True or False in the last run. When a guard is not run because of dict_tag optimization, this leads to false positives. Eg: ```python import torch a = torch.randn(5).cuda() d = {"a": a} def fn(a, d): return a is d["a"], torch.sum(a) cfn = torch.compile(fn) print(cfn(a, d)[0]) print(cfn(a.clone(), d)[0]) ``` Above prints `True` in both cases because of the dict_tag optimization. (`a is d["a"]` is a object aliasing guard which is a relational guard.) In https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/139899, I disabled the dict_tag optimization when Rel...

repository: rapidsai/cuml
title: Cleanup warnings in test suite
github_labels: tests
body_excerpt: Currently a successful `pytest` run of our singlegpu tests logs 900+ warnings. There are a few reasons we might want to intentionally cull these down: - The captured warnings clutter the CI test output, making it harder to find the true source of an issue. - Warnings may indicate problems in our code, or may indicate a problem in the test. Warnings we expect in tests can be silenced per-test (or globally in pytest config). Warnings from our code should be addressed. body_excerpt: I find that I sometimes want to make sure a jitting fails early when being `jit`ted with a tracer where the function requires a concrete value, rather than giving a lengthy stack trace that obfuscates what went wrong. For this, I am using the following methods and thought it might be convenient and instructive to have them be part of the JAX API: ```python def is_tracer(obj: Any) -> bool: return isinstance(obj, jax.core.Tracer) def assert_concrete(obj: Any, obj_name: str = ""): if is_tracer(obj): if not obj_name: obj_name = "<Unnamed>" _msg = f"Object `{obj_name}` needs to be concrete, but was a Tracer. " raise ConcretizationTypeError(obj, _msg) ``` I then use these at the beginning of a function: ```python def test_function(array, concrete_num): assert_concrete(concrete_num, "concrete_num") slicer = min(5, concrete_num) return array[slicer:] ```

title: [FEA] Test estimators with hypothesis
github_labels: feature request|2 - In Progress|? - Needs Triage
body_excerpt: Many of cuml's tests are aimed at comparing results between different implementations, e.g., the GPU and CPU implementation of the same estimator and against third-party implementations, notably scikit-learn. We expect estimators to overall behave very similarly and their results to be identical up to numerical precision. Further, estimators are usually tested only against a specific combination of inputs and example datasets, an approach that likely fails to test rare edge cases and cannot provide confidence for the equivalence of a wide-range of inputs and datasets. Using hypothesis to test estimators and compare results has therefore two positive effects: 1. The API surface is tested significantly more often against edge cases and extreme values. 2. Any validation through the comparison of results is done on a more diverse set of input datasets. A potential downside is an increase in test implementation complexity and test runtime. title: Numerical Discrepancies between Pallas Kernel and Standard JAX with bfloat16
github_labels: bug
body_excerpt: ### Description We are observing small numerical differences between a JAX function compiled with @jax.jit and an equivalent operation implemented as a Pallas kernel when using jnp.bfloat16 data types. The operations involve taking the mean of the squares of a tiled 2D array row-wise, followed by a reciprocal square root. While all intermediate computations within both versions are explicitly cast to jnp.float32, the final results, when cast back to jnp.bfloat16, show differences in a small number of elements. The standard JAX version and the Pallas kernel version produce bit-identical results when the input and output types are jnp.float32. The discrepancies only appear when downcasting the float32 results to jnp.bfloat16. We suspect this might be due to slightly different floating-point summation orders within the jnp.mean operation between XLA's standard optimization and the Pallas/Mosaic tiled execution, leading to minute differences in the float32 results. These differences, although small in float32, cross rounding boundaries when converting to bfloat16, especially after being transformed by lax.rsqrt. body_excerpt: It seems like check_grads has incorrect scaling behaviour for large input tensors. In the code of [check_jvp](https://github.com/google/jax/blob/master/jax/test_util.py#L204) (which is called by [check_grads](https://github.com/google/jax/blob/master/jax/test_util.py#L235)), the following line essentially performs a weighted-sum reduction over `args.size` values: ``` v_out, t_out = f_jvp(args, tangent) ``` The vector `tangent` has a length which grows with the dimension of `args`. This would warrant scaling of tolerances by `args.size`. However, such scaling is not performed. Instead, `t_out` is passed into ``` check_close(t_out, t_out_expected, atol=atol, rtol=rtol) ``` which will eventually call: ``` _assert_numpy_allclose(a, b, atol=atol * a.size, rtol=rtol * b.size) ``` Thus, the scaling will happen by `t_out.size` which is the height of the Jacobian, instead of the width `args.size`, along which the reduction actually happened. Moreover, `_assert_numpy_allclose` actually performs element-wise comparison with the given tolerances and does ``` cond = reduced.all() ``` reduction on a boolean array. title: [FEA] Check convergence before setting fit_status for SVM
github_labels: feature request|? - Needs Triage
body_excerpt: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.** In Sklearn, the fit_status variable of SVM's indicate the following: - 0 means correctly fitted - 1 otherwise, which can also mean that the model is fitted but it did not converge up to the required precision. - The variable is not defined before we fit the model In cuML, currently we have the following implementation: - 0 means fitted, more precisely the fit method returned succesfully. It can still happen that the training was terminated because of reaching `max_iter`, which means that we did not reach the required tolerance. - The variable is not defined before we fit the model **Describe the solution you'd like** Set the fit status to be consistent with Sklearn. We have the number of iterations and the reached tolerance (`diff`) after the solver finished. https://github.com/rapidsai/cuml/blob/396fc69e58800310e2b0de8e3017cf85e4d77207/cpp/src/svm/smosolver.h#L161-L164 We could for example return `n_iter` from SmoSolver in the SvmModel struct, and compare it to max_iter in the python layer to check whether the exit criteria was reaching max iter.

body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** The following `cuml.metrics` clustering metrics change when class/cluster label identities are permuted (e.g., flipping 0 ↔ 1 in the predicted labels), whereas they should be invariant to any permutation of label values: - homogeneity_score - completeness_score - v_measure_score - mutual_info_score According to the scikit-learn definitions that cuML mirrors, these metrics are **independent of the absolute label values**—a permutation of class or cluster labels must not change the score. This is documented for each metric and for the combined function in scikit-learn. issue_body_excerpt: ### Description The following arrays give an apparently incorrect overflowed result with matmul. ```py >>> import cupy as cp >>> x = cp.asarray([51307], dtype=cp.uint16) >>> y = cp.asarray([[[327]]], dtype=cp.uint16) >>> x array([51307], dtype=uint16) >>> y array([[[327]]], dtype=uint16) >>> x @ y # This is giving a different answer array([[172]], dtype=uint16) >>> x*y array([[[173]]], dtype=uint16) >>> x @ y[0] array([173], dtype=uint16) >>> x * y[0] array([[173]], dtype=uint16) ``` The error only occurs when the second array has 3 dimensions. Presumably cupy uses different code paths for stacked vs. non-stacked linear algebra functions. Note that `51307*327 % 2**16` is indeed `173`. I'm unclear whether this behavior is actually a bug or if this is something that is to be expected from overflowing integers. I identified this with the array API test suite, but it is unrelated to the array API module. The array API doesn't specify overflow behavior, but it would be simpler in the test suite if it could just ignore overflowing. ### To Reproduce ```py # Write the code here ``` ### Installation Conda-Forge (`conda install ...`) ### Environment ``` OS : Linux-5.13.0-40-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.34 Python Version : 3.10.4 CuPy Version : 10.4.0 CuPy Platform : NVIDIA CUDA NumPy Version : 1.22.3 SciPy Version : 1.8.0 Cython Build Version : 0.29.28 Cython Runtime Version : None CUDA...
comments_excerpt: Thanks for reporing. I can replicate the error and am looking further... Seems that cupy's matmul computes with cublas gemm routines when ndim > 2. Cublas gemm routines support only floating-point or complex values, so `x @ y` above is computed in float32 then casted back to an integer. However, float32 in IEEE754 representation has only 24-bit precision, thus numbers equal to or larger than 2^24 = 16777216 lose some bits from LSB and get rounded. ```py >>> np.int32(51307*327).astype('H') 173 >>> np.float32(51307*327).astype('H') 172 ```

repository: numba/numba
title: Support For CPU Atomics
github_labels: feature_request
issue_body_excerpt: ## Feature request It would be great if there were a way to use atomic operations from within numba. Currently atomic operations are only supported when generating cuda or HSA code. I'm currently experimenting with using numba to write callbacks that are provided to a C++ concurrency library. In this context, atomics are useful in that they can reduce the amount of synchronization required (or to write the locks that are actually being used). You can technically use atomic operations now if you hide them inside a function pointer exported from C++, but the performance impacts of doing so aren't clear to me. At first glance, preventing inlining seems like a high price to pay for every atomic operation. With regards to what would be the most useful, weak memory consistency is by far the most common thing that shows up in the applications I'm looking at right now, but what's needed is application specific in general. Other consistencies could potentially be useful to me for being able to acquire/release existing locks without having to route everything through an externally compiled function, but that's more of a secondary concern at the moment.
comments_excerpt: FYI I was just looking at this and you can achieve it reasonably with https://gist.github.com/sklam/40f25167351832fe55b64232785d036d (renamed to `numba.extending.intrinsics`), but it requires a bit of llvm work. Neat example! I hadn't seen that before. To document a use case for this feature: the [HogWild! algorithm](http://papers.nips.cc/paper/4390-hogwild-a-lock-free-approach-to-parallelizing-stochastic-gradient-descent) requires atomic floating-point addition. While that may be achievable in Numba's CUDA support, we need atomic intrinsics (ideally applicable to NumPy arrays, an intrinsic atomic `arr[i] += x` operation) in order to make such implementations that work without a GPU. Just wanted to add to this, I’ve felt a need for this when I wanted to: * generate large histograms in parallel (too large to give each thread a copy) * perform GraphBLAS-like parallel graph computations ...

issue_body_excerpt: Triton version: 2.1.0 (nightly build) GPU used: A6000 ### TLDR: With block pointers, loading a block that spills over a dimension boundary, does not respect the `padding_option` specified. ### Details: Below is a minimal reproducible kernel that sums up column blocks of MxN tensor `X`. Say X is 32x32, column block size is 16. This kernel will output a 2x1 Y tensor which contains the sum of all elements in X[:, 0:16] and X[:, 16:32]. Each kernel program instance handles a column to sum up. The below kernel produces correct results when M is a multiple of `block_size` but incorrect otherwise. Using both `padding_option="zero"` or `padding_option="nan"` results in the same incorrect result. The key line below is `x = tl.load(X_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0, 1), padding_option="zero")` ``` import torch import triton.language as tl import triton @triton.jit def sum_col_block(X, Y, M, N, num_col_blocks: tl.constexpr, block_size: tl.constexpr, col_block_size: tl.constexpr): # one program to sum up a column block pid = tl.program_id(axis=0) X_block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(base=X, shape=(M, N), strides=(N, 1), offsets=(0, pid * col_block_size), block_shape=(block_size, col_block_size), order=(1,0)) acc = tl.zeros((1,1), dtype=tl.float32) for _ in range(0, M, block_size): x = tl.load(X_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0, 1), padding_option="zero") s = tl.sum(x, axis=0) s = tl.sum(s, axis=0) ...
comments_excerpt: I believe it's not a bug. Try: ` X_block_ptr = tl.advance(X_block_ptr, (block_size, 0))` I am already using that. ``` for _ in range(0, M, block_size): x = tl.load(X_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0, 1), padding_option="zero") s = tl.sum(x, axis=0) s = tl.sum(s, axis=0) acc += s tl.advance(X_block_ptr, (block_size, 0)) ``` To clarify, `tl.advance` doesn't have side effects, you need to assign the return value to block_ptr. That fixed it! Thanks :-)

title: [RFC] Optimize persistent reduction with `recompute from cached inputs`

issue_body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch **1. Backgroud:** For normalization kernels, e.g. RMS Norm, the inputs are loaded twice, one for reduction, the other for normalization. Inductor generates a persistent reduction which loads inputs to registers for once and cache as float32 for computations. Due to register pressure, this feature is only used when the reduction dimension is small, e.g. <= 1024. [Recent blog](https://pytorch.org/blog/sota-normalization-performance-with-torch-compile/) showed the current SOTA is about 6000GB/s while the max on GB200 is about 7928 GB/s. **2. Proposal: Optimize persistent reduction with recompute from cached inputs** **2. 1 Register cache** (a) Instead of cache inputs as float32, we directly cache them as float16 and only convert to float32 at the time of computation. issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ```python import torch a = torch.rand(4, requires_grad=True) b = a.view(4) assert b.requires_grad and b._is_view() with torch.no_grad(): c = b.view(4) assert c.requires_grad class View(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, x): # return x.data.view(x.shape) return x.detach().view(x.shape) @staticmethod def backward(ctx, grad): return grad d = View.apply(a) assert d.requires_grad and d._is_view() with torch.no_grad(): e = d.view(4) assert e.requires_grad # AssertionError ``` The variable `d` in the `forward` method of other `autograd.Function` implementations may behave differently compared to `b`. But I don’t have any method to distinguish between them. ### Versions Versions of relevant libraries: [pip3] numpy==2.3.4 [pip3] nvidia-cublas-cu12==12.6.4.1 [pip3] nvidia-cuda-cupti-cu12==12.6.80 [pip3] nvidia-cuda-nvrtc-cu12==12.6.77 [pip3] nvidia-cuda-runtime-cu12==12.6.77 [pip3] nvidia-cudnn-cu12==9.10.2.21 [pip3] nvidia-cufft-cu12==11.3.0.4 [pip3] nvidia-curand-cu12==10.3.7.77 [pip3] nvidia-cusolver-cu12==11.7.1.2 [pip3] nvidia-cusparse-cu12==12.5.4.2 [pip3] nvidia-cusparselt-cu12==0.7.1 [pip3] nvidia-nccl-cu12==2.27.5 [pip3] nvidia-nvjitlink-cu12==12.6.85 [pip3] nvidia-nvtx-cu12==12.6.77 [pip3] pytorch-triton==3.5.0+git7416ffcb [pip3] torch==2.10.0.dev20251023+cu126 [pip3] torchvision==0.25.0.dev20251023+cu126 cc @ezyang @albanD @gqche...
comments_excerpt: You should not use `.data` in general. If you want to detach from the autograd graph, you can use `.detach()` But within a custom Function forward, since autograd is already disabled, you can just do return `x.view(x.shape)` @albanD Using `.detach()` can also reproduce this issue, while `x.view(x.shape)` seems to resolve it. repository: jax-ml/jax
title: Initial benchmarking of jax on some simple kernels
github_labels: performance
issue_body_excerpt: I've setup a standard system for comparing various jax JIT backends to hand-written CUDA code. The system is a 3000 particle system, and we're evaluating a fused electrostatic + van Der waals repulsion force. github_labels: feature_request
issue_body_excerpt: This is a "narrative" type of bug report, aka "search the code and compare". No test cases are provided here. Python and NumPy has each changed their `sum()` implementations beyond ordinary linear summation. Specifically: * In https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/100425 (and linked, merged PRs), Python moves to a Neumaier algorithm over the previous naive summation. The slowdown was only 20%, which is probably because all the iterator stuff was taking most of the time... * In the above CPython issue it was mentioned that NumPy does a partial pairwise summation. This provides an improvement of precision in the average case for basically free. (A difference in order was previously noticed in https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/9819#issuecomment-2508969906.) ### Implementation considerations Neumaier is very serial because it has a loop-carried dependency. This can be ameliorated by computing partial sums, which also lends nicely to SIMD. That would introduce some difficulty in numeric reproduction *if* the lane count is dynamically determined. Doing it over the same lane count should always result in the same sequence of operations and be perfectly reproducible. Still, any performant choice (i.e. not 1) would produce results different from upstream. Pairwise is quite amenable to parallelization, from multi-node to multi-core to SIMD. On this path, backward `float16` GEMMs appear to run without the ROCm backward-pass alternative implementation that preserves fp16 subnormals. issue_body_excerpt: ### Description Given the following test case: ``` from absl.testing import absltest from absl.testing import parameterized import chex import jax from jax import numpy as jnp class ScatterDropTest(chex.TestCase): def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): jax.print_environment_info() super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) @parameterized.named_parameters( dict( testcase_name="indices_are_sorted_unique_indices", indices_are_sorted=True, unique_indices=True, ), dict( testcase_name="indices_are_not_sorted_unique_indices", indices_are_sorted=False, unique_indices=True, ), dict( testcase_name="indices_are_sorted_nonunique_indices", indices_are_sorted=True, unique_indices=False, ), dict( testcase_name="indices_are_not_sorted_nonunique_indices", indices_are_sorted=False, unique_indices=False, ), ) def test_scatter_drop( self, indices_are_sorted: bool, unique_indices: bool ): positive_values = ( jnp.full((4,), -1) .at[jnp.array([-1, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, -1, -1])] .set( jnp.arange(8), indices_are_sorted=indices_are_sorted, unique_indices=unique_indices, mode="drop", ) ) chex.assert_trees_all_equal( positive_values, jnp.array([2, 3, 4, 5]) ) if __name__ == "__main__": absltest.main() ``` The expected output is `[2, 3, 4, 5]` but instead `[2, 3, 4, 0]` is returned from the scatter. ### System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.) ``` jax: 0.4.29 jaxlib: 0.4.29 numpy: 1.26.3 python: ...
comments_excerpt: Hi - I think this is working as expected. In three of the cases, you are setting `indices_are_sorted` and/or `unique_indices` to True, when your indices are neither unique nor sorted. If you lie to the compiler, you get undefined results. In the last case where both flags are set to False, the output is also consistent with the documented behavior of the API: you have multiple duplicate indices. From the [`lax.scatter` documentation](https://jax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_autosummary/jax.lax.scatter.html#jax-lax-scatter): > If multiple updates are performed to the same index of operand, they may be applied in any order. `[2, 3, 4, 7]` is a valid output here, because you specified that index `-1` may be set to `7`. Ah, I was expecting that negatives indices would be always out-of-bounds and that out-of-bounds indices would not be counted against `indices_are_sorted` and `unique_indices`...

title: Matrix multiply incorrect for large tensors
github_labels: bug
issue_body_excerpt: ### Description I am pushing this [issue](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/issues/1599) upstream; my guess is it will end up being an XLA issue. I will eventually provide a more minimal example than [this example](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/issues/1599#issuecomment-2677089400) that should end up just being a batched matrix multiply, but it may be worthwhile to make this issue now in case this is a known memory issue. Basically, a simple `vmap_chunked` operator that copies the batching in chunks logic in `jax.lax.map` is used to batch a function that performs a matrix multiplication. When the ``chunk_size`` is large, this matrix multiplication is performed incorrectly. The results are both wrong and not deterministic. In [this example](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/issues/1599#issuecomment-2677089400), the issue occurs when `chunk_size=1000`. The issue vanishes when `chunk_size=100`. Perhaps noteworthy is that the program completes faster than should be possible when the issue occurs. For `chunk_size=1000`, the program completes in 10 seconds and for `chunk_size=100` the program takes 15 minutes. repository: rapidsai/cudf
title: [FEA] libcudf implementation of "intuitive" decimal division
github_labels: feature request
issue_body_excerpt: The `libcudf` implementation of decimal division is really fixed-point division, and does not behave intuitively compared with the accepted conventions in (say) the SQL world. For example, dividing `DECIMAL64(200,-2)` by `DECIMAL64(300,-2)` (which is equivalent to `2.00 / 3.00`) gives a result of `DECIMAL64(0,0)` due to the implementation of `fixed_point<>::operator/()` which simply divides the internal integer values and sets the output scale to the input scale difference. This is not useful in a an SQL context, where the intuitive result would be something like `DECIMAL64(66,-2)` (i.e. `0.66`). While the intuitively-correct behavior *is* achievable using standard `libcudf` operators, for example by pre-scaling the numerator to account for the denominator scale, the required operator graph translation is therefore not 1:1. This has been reported before in this repo, most recently in cuDF issue #17448. For the Velox (and Presto) GPU projects, it was decided to write custom kernels to perform decimal division, in order to achieve the desired behavior in a single operator, although the use of that custom operator is of course limited to "function mode" (i.e. as an alternative to `cudf::binary_operation(X, Y, cudf::binary_operator::DIV)`) and cannot be used by cudf AST mode. These kernels are in Velox PR 16750. Additional custom kernels were implemented to support Presto GPU ag...

repository: numba/numba
title: RFC: Separate NumPy and CPython implementions/functionality.
github_labels: RFC
issue_body_excerpt: This is an RFC on altering Numba's fundamental numerical functionality to better reflect what is present in Python/NumPy. The intended impact of this is to: * Ensure better reproducibility, i.e. Numba will more closely follow what would happen in the interpreter. * Alter performance characteristics with an anticipated net performance gain. * Create conceptually easier paths to follow to achieve higher performance. **Current state:** At present, the Numba code base implements a large number of the functions found in Python builtins, Python's `operator`, `math` and `cmath` modules, and NumPy. Due to historical reasons (largely from the way in which the compiler was bootstrapped) a lot of the implementations of the functions are reasonable approximations for "common" input values that are in use by most users, but they often fail to replicate functionality _exactly_. This "reasonable approximation" has served Numba well, but the current state has a few fundamental problems: 1. The functions often call into each others' implementations, for example NumPy `ufuncs` that "borrow" implementation details from the `math` module. The performance characteristics can be somewhat unpredictable due to this as the implementations from Python modules often contain exception handling whereas NumPy does not. Exceptions lead to branches which lead to lost optimisation opportunities in e.g. vect...

The other way of calculating FLOPS using hlo_module_cost_analysis works but gives a different answer than expected. I applied a Conv block with 2 features with (2,2) kernel size, no bias, "same" padding, (1,1) strides to a (1,4,4,1) array both in flax and keras, then calculated flops used for each. Keras flop calculation would return 256 which makes sense (2 kernels * 16 output cells * (4 mul + 4 sum) = 256). However, both the JAX internal flop calculation tool and the flax flop calculation from the tabulate function return 196 as flops used. How can that be? If we were to dissect the number 196 by dividing it by 2 kernels and 16 output cells, we would get 6.125 flops per cell. The only way I think this would be possible is 4 mul and 2 1/8th add per cell with some sort of vectorization optimization going on? This discrepancy between keras and flax flop count doesn't occur if the padding is "valid". The google colab link includes this short display: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1ClNx5FWMIvf_H_jGVV4Z2T1_9J0ZmNlF?authuser=0#scrollTo=e8mzJ2rvvgRL ### What jax/jaxlib version are you using? jax v0.4.17, jaxlib v0.4.14 ### Which accelerator(s) are you ...

comments_excerpt: In this repro, the function `foo()` is mutating a tensor with overlapping data. This is undefined behavior ([docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.as_strided.html)), because there is a data race to perform the mutation, so you can get different results depending on the kernel that runs, and we end up with a different behavior under eager vs compile. For example if as_strided gives me [[-2,-1],[-1,2]]. The output will be [[-1,1],[1,2]]...

repository: cupy/cupy
title: Discussion on multi-GPU support for cuFFT and cuSOLVER
github_labels: cat:feature|pr-ongoing
issue_body_excerpt: Original context: See #2644. Some of CUDA libraries like cuFFT and cuSOLVER provide native multi-GPU support. However, there is no guarantee that multiple GPUs will outperform single GPU; on the contrary, for cuFFT I found in https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/2644#issuecomment-558835428 that any workload that can be handled in one GPU should ***not*** be processed using multi GPUs; the extra data transfer just kills the performance (even if NVLinks are present). I suspect the same holds for cuSOLVER. Since CuPy operations incurs additional memory overhead, I think it is clear that multi-GPU is useful only when the workload is too large to fit in one GPU. For such excessive workloads, it's better/unavoidable to start from NumPy arrays directly, such as the "NumPy-in, NumPy-out" feature currently implemented in #2644. **This thread is for discussions regarding this feature and other possible alternative strategies.**

The bug doesn't appear when setting `max_num_parallel_iter` to an integer constant, which must mean it's somehow related to the calculation from the memory info.
